title: Fast & Slow Pointers: Find Where a Cycle Starts
oneLiner: Floyd's algorithm in two phases: let fast and slow meet inside the loop, then walk one pointer from the head and one from the meeting point until they meet at the cycle's entrance.
keyTakeaway: If the distance from head to the cycle start is a, then after fast and slow meet, walking a more steps from the meeting point also lands exactly on the cycle start. So reset one pointer to head, move both one step at a time, and the node where they meet is the answer, with O(1) extra space.
explanation:
Given the head of a singly linked list, return the node where a cycle begins, or null if the list ends normally. A cycle means the tail's Next points back to some earlier node instead of null. The easy answer is a hash set of visited nodes: the first node you see twice is the cycle start. That is O(n) time and O(n) space. Floyd's tortoise and hare does it in O(1) space.

Phase 1 is the cycle detection from the middle-of-a-list lesson: slow moves one node per step, fast moves two. If fast reaches null, there is no cycle, so return null. Otherwise fast gains one node on slow every step once both are inside the loop, so it can't jump over slow and they must land on the same node.

Phase 2 finds the entrance. Say the cycle starts a steps from head, the meeting point is b steps past the cycle start, and the cycle has length c. When they meet, slow has walked a + b steps and fast has walked 2(a + b). The extra a + b steps fast took were whole laps of the cycle, so a + b is a multiple of c. That means a is the same as "c - b, plus some whole laps", and c - b is exactly the distance from the meeting point forward to the cycle start. So put one pointer back at head, leave the other at the meeting point, and move both ONE step at a time. After a steps the first pointer reaches the cycle start from outside, and the second reaches it by going around the loop. The node where they first meet is the answer.

Return the node itself, not its value: values can repeat, and the tests check which node you returned. Each test is built from an array of values and pos, the index the tail links back to (-1 for no cycle). Your function never sees pos.

The visualizer draws the list straight, so remember the last node's arrow really goes back to the cycle start named in the first step.

visualizationSteps.message: The last node (6) links back to index 2 (value 3), not to null. Phase 1: slow and fast both start at head.
slow moves 1 to index 1, fast moves 2 to index 2.
slow moves 1 to index 2, fast moves 2 to index 4.
slow moves 1 to index 3, fast moves 2 to index 2.
slow moves 1 to index 4, fast moves 2 to index 4. They're on the same node: there is a cycle.
Phase 2: put slow back at head and leave fast at the meeting point (index 4). Now both move ONE step at a time.
slow -> index 2, fast -> index 2. Same node again.
They meet at index 2 (value 3): that's where the cycle starts. The head was 2 steps from it, and so was the meeting point, going around the loop.

recognitionSignals: A linked list (or any "next" function, like repeatedly applying f(x)) might loop, and you need the point where the loop begins.
O(1) extra space is required, ruling out a visited set.
A sequence of values in a fixed range must repeat somewhere (find the duplicate in an array of n + 1 numbers from 1 to n) and you can treat value -> index as a next pointer.
gotchas: In phase 2 both pointers move ONE step. Keeping fast at two steps breaks the a = c - b argument.
Check fast != null && fast.Next != null before each double step, or a list without a cycle crashes on the last node.
Compare nodes by reference, not by value; duplicate values can make two different nodes look equal.
A single node whose Next is itself is a cycle starting at index 0. Phase 1 must move the pointers before comparing them, or they "meet" at head before moving.
confusableWith: Fast & Slow Pointers: Find the Middle of a Linked List (this track) uses the same two speeds but stops when fast reaches the end. Here a meeting means a cycle, and a second phase is needed to find where it starts.
Hash Map style "seen before" detection finds the same node in one pass but costs O(n) space. Reach for it when space doesn't matter or when there's no single next pointer to follow.

complexity.note: Phase 1 meets within about n steps of slow (fast gains one node per step once both are in the loop); phase 2 walks at most n more. Just two pointers, versus O(n) for a visited set.
